Subject: LABOR. Test the Black-versus-White unemployment claims: 1972–2025/2026 duration; ratio range 1.576 (2020) to 2.560 (1989); 54-year average 2.115; 17 of 54 years below 2.0; 2023 5.5% Black vs 3.3% White = 1.683; 2024 5.9% vs 3.6% = 1.666. Primary sources: BLS Current Population Survey series LNS14000006 and LNS14000003, including FRED where useful.
Claim Verification Table:
| Claim | Verdict | Authoritative Result | Source | Wording Assessment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Duration: 1972–2025/2026 | Confirmed | 1972–2025 (54 years) | BLS CPS (LNS14000006, LNS14000003) | Supportable; accurately reflects the 54-year data span ending in 2025. |
| Ratio Range: 1.576 (2020) to 2.560 (1989) | Confirmed | 1.576 (2020) to 2.562 (1989) | BLS CPS (LNS14000006, LNS14000003) | Supportable; 2020 low is exact (1.5755); 1989 high is within 0.1%. |
| 54-Year Average: 2.115 | Confirmed | 2.114 | BLS CPS (LNS14000006, LNS14000003) | Supportable; matches the calculated mean of annual ratios (1972–2025). |
| 17 of 54 years below 2.0 | Confirmed | 17 years | BLS CPS (LNS14000006, LNS14000003) | Supportable; exact count verified via annual average ratio analysis. |
| 2023: 5.5% Black vs 3.3% White = 1.683 | Partly Confirmed | 5.5% vs 3.3% (Ratio: 1.685) | BLS CPS (LNS14000006, LNS14000003) | Wording is supportable, but internal math (5.5/3.3=1.683) is inconsistent. |
| 2024: 5.9% vs 3.6% = 1.666 | Partly Confirmed | 6.0% vs 3.6% (Ratio: 1.666) | BLS CPS (LNS14000006, LNS14000003) | Wording is supportable; ratio matches the average of monthly ratios. |
Source Notes: All data retrieved from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Current Population Survey (CPS) via the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database. The analysis utilized seasonally adjusted monthly series LNS14000006 (Black or African American) and LNS14000003 (White). Annual ratios were calculated using two methods: the ratio of annual averages and the average of monthly ratios. The manuscript's 54-year metrics (average and count) align with the 1972–2025 period. Calculations for the 54-year average (2.114) and the count of years with a ratio below 2.0 (17 years) were independently verified using annual average data. Specifically, the years with a ratio below 2.0 are 1975, 1976, 2008–2012, and 2016–2025. The 2023 and 2024 claims were found to use the 'average of monthly ratios' method to arrive at 1.683 and 1.666 respectively, despite the stated component percentages being rounded annual averages. Access date: August 31, 2026. [FRED LNS14000006](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/LNS14000006), [FRED LNS14000003](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/LNS14000003).
Priority Issues: 1. The manuscript contains internal mathematical inconsistencies where the stated ratios do not match the result of dividing the stated component percentages (e.g., 5.5% / 3.3% is calculated as 1.683, but mathematically equals 1.667).\n2. The 2024 Black unemployment rate cited (5.9%) is slightly lower than the full-year authoritative average of 6.0% (5.975%), though the resulting ratio (1.666) accurately reflects the annual average of monthly ratios.\n3. The 1989 maximum ratio is cited as 2.560, while current BLS data yields 2.562, likely reflecting minor historical data revisions or vintage differences.

Subject: WEALTH. Test SCF claims: median White non-Hispanic wealth and Black non-Hispanic wealth gaps of $83,000 in 1989, $130,700 in 2013, and $240,100 in 2022 (2022 $285,000 White versus $44,900 Black); ratio movement of 3.2 cents on the dollar since 1989; and parity estimate ~868 years from an observed ratio-change rate of 0.00097/year. Primary source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances data/tables; carefully identify nominal versus inflation-adjusted dollars and household/family category.
Claim Verification Table:
| Claim | Verdict | Authoritative Result | Source | Wording Assessment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1989 Wealth Gap: $83,000 | **Contradicted** | $156,510 (2022$) / $57,500 (Nominal) | Fed SCF Historical Tables (1989) | Unsupportable; $83k matches no SCF median gap. |
| 2013 Wealth Gap: $130,700 | **Partly Confirmed** | $163,970 (2022$) / $130,900 (Nominal) | Fed SCF 2013 Bulletin, Table 2 | Supportable only as a slightly rounded nominal value. |
| 2022 Wealth Gap: $240,100 | **Confirmed** | White: $285,000; Black: $44,900; Gap: $240,100 | Fed SCF 2022 Bulletin, Table 2 | Fully supportable (2022 dollars). |
| Ratio movement: 3.2 cents since 1989 | **Contradicted** | 9.8 cents (1989–2022) / 3.27 cents (1989–2013) | Fed SCF Dataviz / 2022 Bulletin | Misleading; 3.2 cents only covers up to 2013. |
| Parity estimate: ~868 years | **Contradicted** | ~283 years (based on 1989–2022 trend) | Independent Calculation from SCF | Unsupportable; based on stale/misapplied rate. |
| Rate: 0.00097/year | **Contradicted** | 0.00297/year (1989–2022 actual) | Independent Calculation from SCF | Unsupportable; uses 1989–2013 delta over 33 years. |
Source Notes:
Authoritative values are derived from the [Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) 2022 Bulletin](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/october-2023-changes-in-us-family-finances-from-2019-to-2022.htm) and [historical interactive data](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scf/dataviz/scf/chart/#series:Net_Worth;demographic:racecl4;population:1,2;units:median;range:1989,2022). 

**Calculations:**
- **2022 Ratio:** $44,900 / $285,000 = 0.1575$ (15.75 cents on the dollar).
- **1989 Ratio:** $9,910 / $166,420 = 0.0595$ (5.95 cents on the dollar).
- **1989–2022 Ratio Movement:** $0.1575 - 0.0595 = 0.098$ (9.8 cents).
- **Manuscript's 3.2 cent Movement:** Matches the 1989–2013 change ($0.0922 - 0.0595 = 0.0327$).
- **Parity Rate:** $0.032 / 33 \text{ years} = 0.00097/\text{year}$.
- **Corrected Parity Estimate:** $(1.00 - 0.1575) / 0.00297 \approx 283$ years.

Inflation adjustments use the CPI-U-RS as per Fed methodology. Nominal values for 2013 are from the [2013 SCF Bulletin](https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/bulletin/2014/articles/scf/scf.htm). Access date: Sep 01, 2026.
Priority Issues:
1. **Definitional Mismatch (Nominal vs. Real):** The manuscript inconsistently mixes nominal dollars for 1989 and 2013 gaps with inflation-adjusted (2022) dollars for the 2022 gap. This artificially inflates the perceived growth of the wealth gap from $83,000 to $240,100.
2. **Unsupported 1989 Baseline:** The $83,000 gap for 1989 is not supported by SCF data; the nominal gap was ~$57,500 and the inflation-adjusted gap was ~$156,510.
3. **Methodological Error in Parity Estimate:** The 868-year timeline is based on a "ratio-change rate" of 0.00097/year, which was derived by dividing the 1989–2013 ratio increase (3.2 cents) by the full 33-year period (1989–2022). This ignores the significant ratio gains between 2013 and 2022.
4. **Metric Confusion:** The "3.2 cents" figure is a well-known value in economic literature for the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) out of stock wealth, suggesting a potential misattribution of metrics.

Subject: HOUSING. Prioritize Census/ACS, NAR only for its cited 2023 snapshot, CFPB/HMDA, and HUD OIG report 2013-AT-0003.

| Claim | Verdict | Authoritative Result | Source | Wording Assessment |

| 53% of PHAs did not submit Section 3 reports | **Confirmed** | 53.2% (1,650 of 3,102 PHAs) | HUD OIG Report 2013-KC-0002 / 2013-AT-0003 | Supportable; calculation (1,650/3,102) confirms the percentage. |

Racial homeownership gap calculations are based on U.S. Census Bureau Historical Table 16 (CPS/HVS) for 1968 and ACS 1-Year Estimates (Tables B25003A/B) for 2022. The 1968 gap is 24.8 pp (65.9% White vs 41.1% Black). The ACS 2022 gap is 28.9 pp (73.6% White vs 44.7% Black). The 2023 release figure (27.7 pp) is confirmed via the NAR 2023 Snapshot of Race and Home Buying in America (https://www.nar.realtor/research-and-statistics/research-reports/snapshot-of-race-and-home-buying-in-america), which reports 44.7% Black and 72.4% White ownership.

The HMDA denial ratio range (2.01–2.36) is derived from Federal Reserve Bulletin analysis of HMDA data (https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/bulletin/2012/articles/HMDA/default.htm), specifically comparing Black to White denial rates for conventional home-purchase loans. The 2.36 ratio was recorded in 2011 (23.9% Black vs 10.1% White).

The HUD OIG claim is verified against Audit Report 2013-KC-0002 (and regional variant 2013-AT-0003), where investigators found 1,650 of 3,102 PHAs (53.2%) failed to submit required Form HUD-60002 reports.

The 'nine years' reversal claim is supported by Census CPS/HVS data showing the Black homeownership rate in 2013 (43.1%) regressed to 1995 levels (42.7%), effectively erasing the gains made during the nine-year period from 1995 to the 2004 peak (49.1%).
Priority Issues: 1. Definitional Mismatch: The 2023 release gap of 27.7 pp (44.7% vs 72.4%) is from the National Association of Realtors (NAR) 2023 Snapshot, which uses ACS 2021 data, whereas the ACS 2022 1-year data shows a wider gap of 28.9 pp.\n2. Source Attribution: The 53% Section 3 reporting claim is correctly attributed to a 2013 HUD OIG audit, but the primary national report number is 2013-KC-0002; however, 2013-AT-0003 is a related regional audit often cited in conjunction.\n3. Denial Ratio Specificity: The HMDA denial ratio range (2.01–2.36) refers specifically to the disparity between Black and White applicants for conventional home-purchase loans during the 2004–2011 period, peaking in 2011.

Subject: HEALTH. Test: NCHS maternal mortality rates—Black 69.9/100,000 in 2021 and 49.5 versus White 19.0 per 100,000 in 2022 (ratio stated 2.62); Black life expectancy fell 4.0 years, 74.8 in 2019 to 70.8 in 2021, returning to a mid-1990s level; historical maternal mortality comparative ratios 1.48x in 1930 and 2.61x in 2022 and the claimed 1.76-fold widening. Primary sources: CDC/NCHS publications and historical NCHS tables.
Claim Verification Table:
| Claim | Verdict | Authoritative Result | Source | Wording Assessment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Black Maternal Mortality Rate (2021): 69.9/100,000 | **Confirmed** | 69.9 deaths per 100k | NCHS 2021 [1] | Supportable; exact match. |
| Black Maternal Mortality Rate (2022): 49.5/100,000 | **Confirmed** | 49.5 deaths per 100k | NCHS 2022 [2] | Supportable; exact match. |
| White Maternal Mortality Rate (2022): 19.0/100,000 | **Confirmed** | 19.0 deaths per 100k | NCHS 2022 [2] | Supportable; exact match. |
| 2022 Maternal Mortality Ratio (Black/White): 2.62 | **Partly Confirmed** | 2.61 (49.5 / 19.0) | NCHS 2022 [2] | Supportable; minor rounding diff. |
| Black Life Expectancy (2019-2021): Fell 4.0 years | **Confirmed** | 74.8 (2019) to 70.8 (2021) | NCHS Life Tables [3] | Supportable; exact match. |
| Black Life Expectancy (2021): Return to mid-1990s level | **Confirmed** | 70.2 (1996) / 71.1 (1997) | NCHS 1996 [6] | Supportable; aligns with 1996/97. |
| 1930 Maternal Mortality Ratio: 1.48x | **Contradicted** | 1.48x (Neonatal Ratio) | Shin (1975) [5] | **Definitional Mismatch**; applies to neonatal. |
| 1930 to 2022 Widening: 1.76-fold | **Partly Confirmed** | 1.76 (2.61 / 1.48) | Calculation | Supportable math; based on mismatch. |
Source Notes:
Maternal mortality rates for 2021 and 2022 are sourced from the **CDC/NCHS Health E-Stats** series [1] [2]. The 2021 rate for Black women (69.9) and the 2022 rates for Black (49.5) and White (19.0) women are exact matches to the official reports. The 2022 ratio calculation (49.5 / 19.0 = 2.605) rounds to 2.61, slightly differing from the manuscript's 2.62.

Life expectancy data is verified against the **United States Life Tables** for 2019 and 2021 [3]. The 4.0-year decline for the Black population (74.8 in 2019 to 70.8 in 2021) is confirmed. The "mid-1990s level" claim is supportable, as NCHS historical tables show Black life expectancy at 70.2 in 1996 and 71.1 in 1997 [6].

The 1930 ratio of 1.48x was cross-referenced against historical NCHS datasets. While the manuscript applies this to maternal mortality, authoritative sources like **Shin (1975)** and **Singh (2019)** identify 1.48 as the specific Black-White ratio for **neonatal mortality** in 1930 [5] [7]. National maternal mortality in 1930 was reported as 670 per 100,000 live births, but race-specific ratios for that year were not consistently 1.48 [4].

Priority Issues: 1. **Definitional Mismatch (1930 Ratio)**: The manuscript identifies a 1.48x ratio for 1930 as a maternal mortality metric. Authoritative NCHS historical data confirms the 1.48x ratio specifically describes **neonatal mortality** in 1930 [5], whereas maternal mortality disparities in that era were typically higher (e.g., 2.44x by 1940 [4]).\n2. **Comparative Widening Accuracy**: While the 1.76-fold widening calculation (2.61 / 1.48) is internally consistent with the manuscript's figures, it is fundamentally flawed as it compares a 1930 neonatal ratio to a 2022 maternal ratio.\n3. **Rounding Discrepancy (2022 Ratio)**: The manuscript states a 2.62 ratio for 2022; however, primary data (49.5 / 19.0) yields 2.61. The 2.62 figure appears to be a carryover from the 2021 Black/White ratio (69.9 / 26.6 = 2.63) or a slight rounding error.

Subject: EDUCATION. Test NAEP national Grade 8 reading race-gap claims: 1992 White 267.001 minus Black 237.374 = 29.63; 2022 White 268.443 minus Black 243.902 = 24.54; decline of 5.09 points over 30 years; linear parity projection of about 144 years. Primary source: NCES NAEP/Nation's Report Card data service. Also state whether the racial categories and standard errors make the trend framing supportable.
Claim Verification Table:
| Claim | Verdict | Authoritative Result | Source | Wording Assessment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1992 White Score: 267.001 | Confirmed | 267.0013 | NCES Digest Table 221.10 | Supportable; matches unrounded NDE data. |
| 1992 Black Score: 237.374 | Confirmed | 237.3739 | NCES Digest Table 221.10 | Supportable; matches unrounded NDE data. |
| 1992 Race Gap: 29.63 | Confirmed | 29.6274 | Calculated from NCES data | Supportable; rounds to 29.63. |
| 2022 White Score: 268.443 | Confirmed | 268.4427 | NCES Digest Table 221.10 | Supportable; matches unrounded NDE data. |
| 2022 Black Score: 243.902 | Confirmed | 243.9023 | NCES Digest Table 221.10 | Supportable; matches unrounded NDE data. |
| 2022 Race Gap: 24.54 | Confirmed | 24.5404 | Calculated from NCES data | Supportable; rounds to 24.54. |
| Gap Decline: 5.09 points | Confirmed | 5.0870 | Calculated from NCES data | Supportable; rounds to 5.09. |
| Parity Projection: ~144 years | Confirmed | 144.72 years | Calculated from NCES data | Supportable; linear extrapolation is accurate. |
Source Notes:
Authoritative values were extracted from the **NCES Digest of Education Statistics Table 221.10** (2022 Edition), which archives high-precision unrounded data from the **NAEP Data Explorer (NDE)**. The 1992 baseline (267.001 for White students and 237.374 for Black students) reflects the initial national assessment where accommodations were not permitted, whereas the 2022 data reflects the most recent assessment with accommodations permitted. NCES maintains these as a continuous trend for long-term achievement analysis [1](https://nces.ed.gov/programs/digest/d22/tables/dt22_221.10.asp).

The linear parity projection was calculated by determining the annual rate of gap closure. The gap narrowed from 29.6274 points in 1992 to 24.5404 points in 2022, a total decline of 5.0870 points over 30 years. This yields an average annual closure rate of 0.1696 points. Dividing the remaining 2022 gap (24.54) by this rate results in a projection of approximately 144.7 years to reach parity, confirming the manuscript's "about 144 years" estimate.

Statistical supportability was assessed using the reported standard errors (SE). The 1992 gap SE was approximately 2.01, and the 2022 gap SE was 0.65. The z-score for the 5.09-point change is approximately 2.41 (p ≈ 0.016), which meets the standard threshold for statistical significance (p < 0.05). While racial category definitions were refined in 2011 to include "Two or More Races," NCES maintains that the "White" and "Black" (non-Hispanic) trend lines remain supportable for longitudinal comparisons [2](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/reading/nation/groups/?grade=8).
Priority Issues: None identified. All numerical assertions match high-precision authoritative data from the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), and the resulting trend framing is statistically supportable.

Subject: HISTORY_AND_AGRICULTURE. Test: Slave Voyages figures 12,521,337 embarked, 10,702,656 disembarked in the Americas, difference 1,818,681 and 14.5% mortality, and North American disembarkation 388,747 (3.6%). Separately test the Black-owned farmland claim: decline from a 1910 peak of 13.5 million acres to 1.5 million acres in 1997, described as 90% loss. Use the database / USDA sources appropriate to each and flag whether wording 'passed out of Black hands' is supported.

| **Slave Voyages**: 1,818,681 difference | **Confirmed** | 1,818,681 | TSTD (Calculation) [1] | Supportable |

| **Slave Voyages**: 388,747 N. Amer. disembark. | **Confirmed** | 388,747 | SlaveVoyages.org [1] | Supportable |
| **Slave Voyages**: 3.6% N. Amer. share | **Confirmed** | 3.63% | TSTD (Calculation) [1] | Supportable |
| **Farmland**: 1910 peak of 13.5m acres | **Partly Confirmed** | 12.8m - 16m acres | USDA ERS [5]; NRHP [4] | Discrepancy: 13.5m is 1900 Southern figure |
| **Farmland**: 1.5m acres in 1997 | **Confirmed** | 1.5m acres | 1997 USDA Census [3] | Supportable |
| **Farmland**: 90% loss since peak | **Confirmed** | ~90% | ProPublica [2]; FoodPrint [6] | Supportable |

Source Notes:
The figures for the transatlantic slave trade were verified using the **Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (TSTD)**, specifically the **Estimates** section, which provides a comprehensive assessment of the trade between 1501 and 1866 [1]. The mortality rate calculation (1,818,681 dead / 12,521,337 embarked) yields **14.52%**, confirming the manuscript's 14.5% figure as a supportable rounding. Similarly, the North American disembarkation rate (388,747 / 10,702,656) is **3.63%**, supporting the 3.6% claim [1].

For agricultural data, the **1997 USDA Census of Agriculture** confirms that Black farmers owned **1.5 million acres** of farmland [3]. The 1910 "peak" of 13.5 million acres appears to be a slight misattribution of the **1900 Southern peak** (13.5 million acres) to the 1910 date, as the **1910 Census** recorded 12.8 million acres for owners in the South [5]. The description of a **90% loss** is a standard characterization in academic and governmental literature, representing the decline from approximately 15-16 million acres at the height of ownership to the 1.5 million reported in 1997 [2] [6]. The wording **"passed out of Black hands"** is considered supportable, as it reflects the documented systemic factors—including discriminatory lending, heirs' property vulnerabilities, and involuntary foreclosures—that drove the decline [2].

Source Notes:
Demographic data for St. James Parish and Humphreys County were sourced from the **U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts** and **American Community Survey (ACS)** 5-year estimates. St. James Parish District-level data was cross-referenced with the [Statistical Atlas of the United States](https://statisticalatlas.com/Louisiana/St-James-Parish/Race-and-Ethnicity), which confirms high Black population densities (up to 90.6%) in specific tracts within District 5.

The **EPA EJScreen** removal was verified via multiple reports from environmental data organizations such as [EnviroDataGov](https://envirodatagov.org/epa-removes-ejscreen-from-its-website/) and [Harvard Law's EELP Tracker](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/tracker/epa-added-environmental-health-indicators-to-ejscreen/), confirming the discontinuation of public access on February 5, 2025.

Humphreys County health statistics were verified using the [CDC PLACES](https://www.cdc.gov/places/index.html) 2024 release, which provides model-based estimates for chronic diseases. The hypertension rate of 51.2% reported by [WJTV](https://www.wjtv.com/living-local/focused-on-health/counties-with-the-highest-rates-of-high-blood-pressure-in-mississippi/) closely aligns with the manuscript's 51.7% claim. The 2013 closure of Patients' Choice Medical Center in Belzoni is widely documented in local news archives, including [Mississippi Today](https://mississippitoday.org/2026/07/16/county-lost-hospital/).

Population loss calculations for Humphreys County were based on the 1980 Census figure of 13,931 (cited in the [Mississippi Encyclopedia](https://mississippiencyclopedia.org/entries/humphreys-county/)) compared to the 2024 ACS estimate of 7,785. The resulting 44.1% decline exceeds the "one-third" claim. Housing vacancy for Humphreys County was calculated as (Total Units - Occupied Units) / Total Units using 2024 ACS data (3,509 total, 2,900 occupied), yielding 17.4%.
